An HTTP cookie (also called web cookie, Internet cookie, browser cookie, or simply cookie) is a small piece of data sent from a website and stored on the user's computer or mobile device by the user's web browser while the user is browsing. Cookies allows us to offer the best services possible by allowing us to recognise you as a unique user and provide us with information about how you use our website. Cookies are commonly used on the Internet and do not harm your computer system. What information do we collect from cookies? Information collected may include items such as the IP address of your computer, the time you visited our website and what links you clicked on or when you opened our emails. However, any information collected is kept secure and only used for the purposes set out in this Privacy and Cookie Policy. Cookies DO NOT collect the following data: Names Phone Numbers Email Addresses Mailing Addresses Bank Account Numbers Credit Card Information What do we use the information we collect from cookies for? Web analytics – To understand how you use our website and to assist us in tailoring the website to customer needs. Website management – Collating anonymous aggregated information that is used to manage and plan enhancements to our services. Source tracking – To evaluate the effectiveness of our advertising and promotions on third party websites, for example by tracking whether these advertisements are clicked on by users. How can I stop cookies and what effect will this have? You can stop cookies from being deployed on your computer by configuring your browser not to accept them. However, in order to get the best use out of our website you will need to have cookies enabled. Please be aware that deleting certain cookies can result in difficulties when navigating around sites. In most cases, the Lurcher is born from the sighthound dog breed, which is where its intelligence comes from, and the Greyhound, known for its powerful legs and speed. In the past, the Lurcher was the most popular poacher’s dog. But, as time went by, they became common hunting and racing dogs, as well as at-home pets. Because of the different breed combinations, the appearance and size of this dog will vary. Overall, the Lurcher has a lean and long body with muscular legs and super deep chests. 12 - 15 years Lifespan 60cm Size 15 - 45kg Weight 3/5 Cold weather tolerance 4/5 Hot weather tolerance 1 hour + a day Exercise Short Coat 2/5 Dog Friendly Behaviour and personality The Lurcher is a very intelligent dog. It is also affectionate and demonstrative at the same time. They can think on their own without the owner giving them directions which is what makes them a lot smarter than highly obedient breeds. But, when you want to teach them new commands, training can get tricky. Since they are not used to picking up human direction and go against their instincts, it can take a while to train a Lurcher. Not because they lack the intelligence, but because they are not used to moving without their independence. A Lurcher creates a lively litter and a happy but exhausted owner. As a puppy, the Lurcher is often fast, agile, and full of energy. When they grow up, their social side tends to flourish. They become faster, stronger, and more determined. Although they can make a mess at times, they will constantly bring joy and amusement. Once trained, this dog breed will respond well to commands. Ideal owner / home House with a garden Experienced owner Plenty of open space This dog breed will savour every moment of a long walk, especially if you give them the opportunity to run in a safe and large area. However, this dog may not be the best pet if you have rabbits and cats running around. Because of its nature, the dog will instinctively chase these animals, regardless of how long they have been in the house. Being an independent thinker makes it quite difficult to teach them to control these impulses. Grooming Their coat type and size vary based on the cross they came from. Sometimes, the coat can be smooth, at other times, rough. Overall, a Lurcher is a short coat dog with limited shedding. That’s why it is not high maintenance. Brushing around once a week can get rid of all that dead hair and keep the coat nice and smooth. Short-haired breeds are a popular choice among people who are sensitive to dog hair. Other than that, you will be doing basic care, like the monthly trim, ear cleaning, and drying. When checking their ears, you should look out for redness, bad smells, and dirt. If your canine friend loves to run around in the fields or garden, make sure you check for ticks and fleas regularly. Regular oral hygiene is also necessary, especially if you want your dog to have a fresh breath and a healthy smile. When it comes to weather, there are a couple of things to think about. Firstly, thanks to their short hair, they tend to get cold relatively quickly. Secondly, whilst the Lurcher does prefer warmer periods, it is important to let them rest away from direct sunlight and extremely hot temperatures to avoid sun burn and heat stroke. Health Just like any other dog breed, the Lurcher is also susceptible to some genetic health issues. To help protect your pet if they do develop a health condition, you can get Lurcher Pet Insurance. In general, these dogs are a very healthy crossbreed. They are strong dogs but can experience muscle or foot injuries, heatstroke, gastric torsion, etc. If their ancestry had eye problems, the odds of the dog developing them could get higher. Thyroid evaluation is also necessary. It can give you a good perspective of the dog's health state and general well-being. Obesity is another common problem so it’s important that they are given a healthy diet and regular exercise. With adequate weight, you can easily extend its lifespan and let them enjoy a fuller and healthier life. Common health issues Gastric Dilatation Volvulus (Gastric Torsion or Bloat) Bloat doesn’t sound too serious, but if it’s left untreated it can be deadly for your dog. Large, deep-chested dogs are more commonly affected than smaller breeds. Bloat causes the stomach to swell with gas and then twist. The dog can’t belch or vomit to release the gas, blood flow to the heart is impeded, blood pressure drops, and the dog goes into shock. To avoid bloat, split their feeds into multiple smaller meals through the day instead of one large portion. You must also avoid exercise for at least half an hour to an hour after eating. Another cause can be drinking too much water rapidly, so keep a watchful eye on that as well. Symptoms of Gastric Dilation Volvulus are a swollen abdomen, excessive drooling, dry retching, lethargy and a rapid heart rate. Without immediate medical attention, bloat can be fatal, so if you notice any of these symptoms, take your dog to the vet immediately. Osteosarcoma Osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone cancer that generally affects large and giant breeds. The first symptom is lameness which can be caused by multiple issues, so your dog will need x-rays to determine if the cause is cancer. Treatment for Osteosarcoma is aggressive, usually culminating in amputation of the affected limb, and chemotherapy, but with successful treatment, you can expect your dog to live an extra 9 months to 2 years, perhaps even longer. Luckily, dogs adapt well to life on three legs and don’t suffer the same side effects to chemotherapy as humans, such as nausea and hair loss.
